stops.name: Autun, born into the kin of the Carolingians
stops.campa: Thierry, count of Autun, and his wife Aldana bring a son into the world in the hill country of Burgundy, kin by blood to the house that will crown Charlemagne. The chroniclers give no day, only the century's turning decade. He is called Guilhem in the tongue of the south he will make his own, Willehalm in the tongue of the poets who will carry him three centuries forward as a name the whole Rhine and Rhone will recognize. Nothing yet marks him; the marches of Septimania and the towers of a grail he cannot imagine wait beyond the Pyrenees and the Vosges both.

stops.name: Toulouse, ward and count: the boy-king's guardian
stops.campa: Charlemagne names Guilhem Count of Toulouse, the frontier post nearest the Andalusian marches, and sets him beside the child Louis, crowned sub-king of Aquitaine at three years old and now growing toward manhood inside walls the Saracens test every campaigning season. Guilhem drills the boy in arms and counsel both, the elder cousin standing where a father should. The Astronomer, who will one day write Louis's own life, remembers Guilhem's name among the magnates who raised the prince who will become emperor. Neither of them yet knows how long the debt of this schoolroom will run.

stops.name: The Orbieu, the field lost and the march held
stops.campa: Hisham I's army sweeps into Septimania in the campaigning season, and Guilhem meets them on the banks of the Orbieu below Narbonne. The field goes against him: the annals record a Frankish rout, kinsmen and vassals cut down around him, the count himself barely escaping the press. But the invaders, bled white by the stand, turn back toward Barcelona rather than press on to Toulouse or Narbonne. The marches hold because the price of breaking them was made too high on this one river's bank. Guilhem carries the defeat home and rebuilds the line through the winter.

stops.name: Narbonne, the muster of Aquitaine and Provence
stops.campa: For the siege the young king Louis is ordering against Barcelona, Guilhem gathers the levies of his own march: Franks, Goths, Provençals, Basques and Aquitanians mustering under Narbonne's walls before the long road south. He is the seasoned hand among the captains, the one who has already lost a field to this enemy and knows what the crossing of the passes will cost. The army that forms here will sit before Barcelona through the autumn and winter, starving the city rather than storming it, a patience Guilhem argues for out of his own hard lesson at the Orbieu.

stops.name: Barcelona, the city starved into surrender
stops.campa: After a siege of months the governor Sa'dun surrenders Barcelona to Louis and Guilhem without a final assault, the granaries exhausted before the walls are breached. Guilhem rides in among the first captains, the frontier he has bled for pushed at last past the Pyrenees into Spain itself. Ermold the Black will later set the whole campaign in verse for the emperor's court, naming Guilhem among the great of the army. It is the summit of his career as a count of the sword, and, though none present can know it, the last such summit the ordinary chronicles will fully credit to him.

stops.name: Gellone, the abbey founded in the desert gorge
stops.campa: In the wild gorge below Aniane, where the Verdus stream cuts through white stone, Guilhem founds a monastery and endows it with land and church plate, placing it under the rule of his friend Benedict of Aniane. Among the gifts he lays on the altar is a splinter of the True Cross, sent to him by his cousin Charlemagne. The place will take his own name after his death, Saint-Guilhem-le-Désert, the desert of Saint William, though on this day it is simply Gellone, a count's retreat built while the count is still very much a man of the world.

stops.name: Gellone, the cowl taken, the sword laid down
stops.campa: Two years after founding it, Guilhem resigns Toulouse and enters his own abbey as a monk, exchanging the count's mantle for the habit, carrying his own building stone up from the river with the other brothers, by the tradition's telling, so that no labor of the house is beneath him. Benedict of Aniane's strict rule governs the cloister; Guilhem submits to it as he once submitted to the discipline of the march. The warrior who broke at the Orbieu and stood at Barcelona now keeps silence, works the terraces, and waits on God the way he once waited on the Saracen advance.

stops.name: Gellone, the terminus the world's chronicles record
stops.campa: On this day, by the calendar every later martyrology and the Church itself will keep, the monk-count dies at Gellone and is buried before his own altar; some copies of the record push the date two years further, to 814, but all agree the story closes here. This is the terminus the ordinary chronicles give, and the terminus his own witness, Kyot, will later refuse. The world writes its epitaph and moves on into Louis's reign; the deeper current the poets will one day call Willehalm's own report runs past this stone unbroken, carrying the man another thirty-six years into events no chronicle here anticipates.

stops.name: Oransche, Arabel won: the city and the bride
stops.campa: Between the wars the tradition sets the winning of Oransche: Willehalm takes the city on the Rhone from King Tybalt, and with it the queen Arabel, who leaves faith, crown, and husband to be baptized Gyburc and become his wife. The Glorieta tower becomes their house. Every grief that follows on the plain of Alischanz is already contained in this one wedding, for Tybalt's kin will cross the sea to take back the woman and the march both. The chansons will sing the taking of Orange for four centuries; Wolfram will hold the marriage up instead, love strong enough to answer for a war.

stops.name: Aachen, the pupil crowned, the tutor recalled
stops.campa: Louis, the boy Guilhem once schooled in the Toulouse garrison, now sits sole emperor at Aachen, his father three years in the grave. War gathers again in the south: King Tybalt's kin muster against the March of Provence, where Willehalm now holds the border and keeps, by the epic's account, a converted wife once named Arabel and now called Gyburc. Word runs north to the imperial court that the march is threatened. Louis remembers the man who raised him at Toulouse and marks him for the coming call, not knowing the summons will run through the oldest debt either of them carries.

stops.name: Alischanz, the first field, Vivianz slain
stops.campa: On the plain the poets call Alischanz, Willehalm's own host meets Tybalt's army and is broken. His young nephew Vivianz, sent ahead with the vanguard, fights to the last blade rather than yield and dies calling on God with his own hand pressed to his wound, a death the epic holds up for two centuries as the pattern of a Christian knight's end. Willehalm alone of the great captains rides clear of the slaughter, Gyburc's city of Oransche shut behind him with his wife inside it, and turns his horse north, not toward safety but toward Aachen and the debt owed him by an emperor he once carried on his own shoulder.

stops.name: Aachen, before the throne, the plea answered
stops.campa: Willehalm rides into Aachen still bloodied from the field, forces his way past the chamberlains, and stands before Louis to demand the relief he is owed, the epic sparing nothing of the emperor's hesitation or the old tutor's fury at finding gratitude so slow. Louis grants the host at last. It is, the poem insists on remembering, the pupil paying the debt of the schoolroom at Toulouse, arms instead of grammar, thirty years returned in a single audience. Willehalm rides south again at the head of a second, larger army, Gyburc still holding Oransche's walls against Tybalt's siege behind him.
